notes.lr-flaw-honors-scholarship-conditional: Two defensible answers. The inference actually runs through the probation premise: 'never on probation' is a necessary condition for completing honors, and the argument treats it as sufficient (A). But the conclusion is also the straight converse of premise 1 (scholarship recipients -> honors), which B describes. A is the more precise description of the inferential step the argument makes; B describes the shape of the conclusion. Recommend tightening so only one choice names the operative flaw (e.g., drop or rewrite B).
notes.lr-flaw-deficit-two-options: Two defensible answers. The 'must either cut spending or raise taxes' claim is stated as a premise, so on strict LSAT convention B (false dilemma) is less attackable than D, which names an unaddressed gap (cuts might also deepen the slowdown). Chose D, but many strong test-takers will pick B. Consider rewording the premise or B so the dilemma is unmistakably given rather than assumed.
notes.lr-flaw-painting-value-senses: E (equivocation on 'value': aesthetic vs. monetary/historical) is the intended structural flaw and the best answer, but C (viewers' knowledge that a work is a reproduction diminishes the experience) is a genuine and fairly direct objection to the key premise. C is attackable as 'disputing a premise' rather than naming a reasoning flaw, but it is closer than a typical wrong answer.
notes.lr-flaw-sleep-grades-start-times: B (third-variable/correlation-causation) is the best answer, but C (later start times are the only way to get more sleep) is also a real gap in the leap from 'more sleep' to 'later start times.' Acceptable as-is; B is clearly the primary flaw, noting only that C is stronger than an ideal distractor.
